name: Ridge Regression
analogy: Think of it as a team of analysts who all say nearly the same thing. A plain model lets them shout over each other with huge, opposite weights; ridge makes them share the work evenly and keeps every voice small, so the forecast stops swinging wildly from bar to bar.

steps.title: Write the forecast as a weighted sum
steps.description: Each feature gets a weight and the forecast is the sum of feature times weight plus a starting level. This is the same recipe as ordinary linear regression.
steps.inExample: The 6-bar-ahead MNQ move is forecast from 35 base features that include several overlapping momentum measures.

steps.title: Rescale the features
steps.description: The brake on the weights treats them all alike, so the features need a common scale first. Each is rescaled using only past bars.
steps.inExample: The 35 features are each rescaled to a similar typical size with trailing statistics.

steps.title: Add a brake on the size of the weights
steps.description: The model is told to keep forecast misses small and also to keep the weights small, paying a cost that grows quickly for large weights. Squaring the weights means one giant weight costs far more than many small ones.
steps.inExample: A penalty strength is set so that no single momentum weight is allowed to grow far beyond the others.

steps.title: Share the weight among overlapping features
steps.description: When two features carry almost the same information, the brake splits the weight evenly between them. Plain regression might give one a huge positive weight and the other a huge negative one, which cancel on the training bars but fail on new ones.
steps.inExample: Three overlapping momentum features each take a moderate weight rather than two exploding in opposite directions.

steps.title: Choose the brake strength on later data
steps.description: The strength is chosen by testing on bars after the training period. Too weak and the weights still swing; too strong and every weight collapses toward zero and the forecast becomes flat.
steps.inExample: Across walk-forward folds the strength with the smallest held-out miss is kept.

steps.title: Forecast with the shrunk weights
steps.description: A new bar is scored as feature times weight, added up. Every feature still has some weight, only smaller and steadier than in the plain version.
steps.inExample: The 14:35 bar is scored and the forecast is a rise of 3 points.

useFor.example: Fitting a 30-minute forecast from several momentum and trend measures on different windows that are strongly related.

useFor.task: A steadier baseline than plain regression
useFor.example: Using it as the linear reference in walk-forward tests because its forecasts change less from fold to fold.
Daily models with dozens of features and only a few thousand bars, where plain regression overfits.

useFor.task: Measuring how much information the features share
useFor.example: Seeing how forecast quality changes as the brake strengthens, as a test of whether the indicators carry separate information.

avoidWhen: You want to remove useless features entirely; ridge keeps all of them with small weights, while lasso or ElasticNet sets some exactly to zero.
The signal needs combined conditions or curves; a weighted sum cannot represent them.
You need a probability of a yes-or-no outcome; logistic regression is the natural choice.

example.scenario: A 5-minute MNQ bar closes at 14:35. A fitted ridge regression forecasts the change in the close 6 bars (30 minutes) later, in points.

input.summary: One row of rescaled features for the bar that just closed.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The price at which the 14:35 five-minute bar closed.

fields.name: relative strength index, 14 bars
fields.meaning: A momentum reading from 0 to 100; under 30 is commonly read as oversold.

fields.name: return over the last 6 bars
fields.value: down about a third of a percent
fields.meaning: How much price has fallen over the previous 30 minutes.

fields.name: return over the last 12 bars
fields.meaning: How much price has fallen over the previous hour, closely related to the 6-bar return.

fields.name: distance from the 50-bar moving average
fields.meaning: How far the close sits below its recent average price.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar.

output.summary: One forecast number and the largest shares of it.

fields.name: forecast change in the close after 6 bars
fields.meaning: The sum of every feature times its shrunk weight, plus the starting level.

fields.name: share from the two overlapping returns
fields.meaning: The combined contribution of the 6-bar and 12-bar returns, which split their weight evenly.

fields.name: forecast in US dollars per contract
fields.meaning: 3 points times 2 US dollars per MNQ point, before any trading costs.

example.reading: The forecast is a faint lean of 3 points. The value of ridge is that it would barely change if you added a 9-bar return alongside the others. Compare it with plain regression on the same folds, and trade it only if the net result after commission and slippage holds up.
